title: Trusting God When Nothing Makes Sense
paragraphs:
Trusting God When Nothing Makes Sense
The Deeper Meaning of Proverbs 3:5–6 and the Journey from Scandal to Grace
There are moments in life when everything looks fine on the outside, yet inside you feel completely lost.
You pray, but heaven seems silent.
You plan carefully, yet doors keep closing.
You try to obey God, but your circumstances become harder instead of easier.
You wonder if you missed His voice.
You wonder if you made the wrong decision.
You wonder why the path ahead feels darker than the one you left behind.
Most people never say these things out loud. They smile. They post encouraging verses. They tell everyone they are blessed.
But in the quiet moments of the night, they wrestle with a question that has haunted humanity since the beginning:
"Can I really trust God when I don't understand what He is doing?"
That question is exactly where Proverbs 3:5–6 meets us.
Not in our certainty.
Not in our strength.
Not in our victories.
But in our confusion.
The passage reads:
"Trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge Him, and He will make straight your paths." (Proverbs 3:5–6, ESV)
For many people, these words have become familiar.
Too familiar.
Quoted on coffee mugs.
Printed on wall decorations.
Shared in social media posts.
But familiarity can sometimes hide the breathtaking depth of what God is actually saying.
The Hebrew text begins with the word "בְּטַח" (betach), translated "trust."
This is not casual belief.
This is not intellectual agreement.
This is not optimism.
The Hebrew carries the idea of complete confidence, secure reliance, placing your full weight upon something because you believe it will hold you.
Imagine standing on a bridge suspended over a deep canyon.
You may say you trust the bridge.
But true trust is revealed when you actually step onto it.
Biblical trust always involves surrender.
The verse continues:
"Trust in Yahweh with all your heart."
The word translated "heart" is the Hebrew "לֵב" (lev).
In biblical thought, the heart was not merely the center of emotions.
It was the center of the entire person.
Mind.
Will.
Desires.
Decisions.
Thoughts.
Affections.
God is not asking for partial trust.
He is not asking for Sunday trust.
He is not asking for emergency trust only when life falls apart.
He is asking for all of you.
Every fear.
Every question.
Every dream.
Every wound.
Every plan.
Every secret.
Every scar.
Trust Him with all your heart.
Then comes the hardest part.
"And do not lean on your own understanding."
The Hebrew word for "lean" literally paints the picture of supporting yourself against something.
Depending upon it.
Resting your weight on it.
Building your confidence upon it.
God is not condemning wisdom.
Scripture consistently praises wisdom.
Rather, God is confronting our tendency to enthrone our own perspective above His.
Human understanding is limited.
God's understanding is infinite.
We see moments.
He sees eternity.
We see pain.
He sees purpose.
We see the chapter.
He sees the entire story.
The prophet Isaiah records God's words:
"For My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways My ways." (Isaiah 55:8)
How many of us have suffered because we demanded that God explain Himself before we obeyed Him?
How many blessings were delayed because we insisted on understanding everything first?
How many miracles were missed because we trusted our calculations more than His promises?
The deeper truth is this:
We often trust ourselves more than we trust God.
That is the scandal hidden inside every human heart.
From Eden onward, humanity has wrestled with the temptation to become its own authority.
The serpent's deception was not merely about fruit.
It was about trust.
Would Adam and Eve trust God's wisdom?
Or their own?
The tragedy of Genesis begins where Proverbs warns us not to go.
Leaning on our own understanding.
And yet this is where the Gospel becomes beautiful.
Because Jesus came to redeem what humanity destroyed.
Where Adam failed, Christ succeeded.
Where humanity rebelled, Christ obeyed.
Where we grasped for control, Christ surrendered completely to the Father.
In the Garden of Gethsemane, facing unimaginable suffering, Jesus prayed:
"Not My will, but Yours, be done." (Luke 22:42)
The Greek word translated "will" is "θέλημα" (thelēma), referring to desire, purpose, intention.
Jesus entrusted Himself fully to the Father's plan even when that plan led through suffering.
The cross itself looked like failure.
It looked like defeat.
It looked like scandal.
But God was writing redemption through what appeared hopeless.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
That is the heartbeat of Proverbs 3.
Trust God even when the story makes no sense.
Because God specializes in rewriting stories.
The greatest proof is Calvary.
A Roman cross became the throne of salvation.
A public execution became the doorway to eternal life.
A scandal became grace.
The empty tomb forever declared that God's purposes are bigger than our understanding.
This is why Proverbs 3:6 says:
"In all your ways acknowledge Him."
The Hebrew word translated "acknowledge" is "יָדַע" (yada).
It means far more than simply knowing facts.
It carries the idea of intimate relationship.
Deep personal knowledge.
Experiential fellowship.
God is not merely asking us to consult Him occasionally.
He is inviting us into continual relationship.
Every decision.
Every conversation.
Every opportunity.
Every struggle.
Every season.
Every step.
Acknowledge Him.
Walk with Him.
Know Him.
Trust Him.
And then comes the promise:
"He will make straight your paths."
Notice what the verse does not say.
It does not promise an easy path.
It does not promise a painless path.
It does not promise immediate answers.
It does not promise a life free from tears.
It promises direction.
God straightens paths that would otherwise lead to destruction.
He guides.
He corrects.
He redirects.
He protects.
He leads.
Sometimes through valleys.
Sometimes through storms.
Sometimes through waiting.
But always toward His glory and our ultimate good.
Many people reading this today are carrying silent burdens.
You are exhausted.
Disappointed.
Confused.
You thought life would look different by now.
You thought God would answer sooner.
You thought healing would come faster.
You thought the breakthrough would already have happened.
Yet here you are.
Still waiting.
Still praying.
Still wondering.
Can I remind you of something?
God has never lost control of your story.
Not once.
Not for a second.
Not even in the chapters that feel unbearable.
The same God who parted the Red Sea.
The same God who preserved Joseph through betrayal.
The same God who restored Peter after failure.
The same God who raised Jesus from the dead.
Is still writing your story.
And He has never abandoned a single page.
Maybe that is why Proverbs 3:5–6 remains one of the most beloved passages in Scripture.
Because every generation discovers the same truth.
Life often refuses to make sense.
But God remains trustworthy.
Even when we cannot trace His hand, we can trust His heart.
Even when we cannot understand His plan, we can trust His character.
Even when the road is dark, we can trust the One who already stands at the destination.
And perhaps that is exactly what someone reading this needs today.
Not another explanation.
Not another strategy.
Not another self-help formula.
Just a reminder that Jesus Christ is worthy of your trust.
Completely.
Fully.
Without reservation.
Because the cross has already proven His love.
The resurrection has already proven His power.
And His faithfulness has never failed.
If this message spoke to your heart, don't keep it to yourself.
You may never know whose faith is hanging by a thread and who needs this reminder today.
Sometimes one shared message becomes the encouragement God uses to reach a weary soul.
What area of your life is God teaching you to trust Him with right now?
Your testimony may encourage someone else who feels alone.
One day you will discover that the chapters you begged God to remove became the very pages He used to reveal His grace.
